title: Explicit State Elicitation Is Not Enough: A Controlled Audit of Memory-Policy Classification

analysis.tldr: This controlled audit shows that asking a model to emit an explicit intermediate memory-state label does not by itself improve Use/Ignore/Update/Ask policy decisions: taxonomy instructions help, but structured state outputs are often non-causal label conditioning and can even hurt when richer semantic evidence is elicited.
analysis.problem: Memory-policy systems often introduce interpretable intermediate labels and assume the explicit state causes better downstream decisions. Existing datasets can be lexically separable, lack positive Ignore examples, or make label→policy mappings deterministic, so apparent interpretability can be mistaken for mechanism.
analysis.core_idea: Rebuild the evaluation as 40 matched four-way counterfactual families (160 examples) with byte-identical task text inside each family and rule-derived policy labels. Compare clean, taxonomy-only, state-output, forced-label, and semantic-evidence variants so the causal value of the intermediate representation can be separated from instruction/label conditioning.

memory_design.write: No persistent store is introduced; the audit constructs controlled counterfactual memory-policy examples.
memory_design.organize: Memory situations are categorized into four decision policies and matched families that hold task wording fixed while varying the relevant memory state.
memory_design.read: Models classify whether retrieved memory should be Used, Ignored, Updated, or trigger Ask; interventions vary whether taxonomy, explicit labels, or semantic evidence are elicited first.
memory_design.update_forget: The paper evaluates classification rather than executing store mutation, response generation, or long-running memory updates.

compared_to: Clean policy classification without intermediate state
Forced correct/wrong intermediate labels and semantic-evidence elicitation
analysis.evidence: On the controlled 160-example set, Llama improves from 44.0 clean to 53.1 with taxonomy-only prompting, while explicit state output is 44.6 (+0.6, p=.808). GPT-OSS rises 54.8→59.8 with taxonomy and to 58.1 with explicit state (+3.3, p=.071; Holm .142). Forced labels shift predictions, but labels map deterministically to policies, showing sensitivity rather than a causal mechanism. A Llama semantic-evidence follow-up scores 55.8 versus 63.3 for policy-only prompting (-7.5; Holm .0146).
analysis.why_it_matters: The paper is a useful negative control for agent-memory interfaces: a readable intermediate field is not automatically a useful state variable. Intermediate representations should be justified by matched downstream gains, not by interpretability or sensitivity alone.
limitations: The study stops at policy classification and does not measure final response quality, tool actions, or actual memory mutation.
The matched set is small and synthetic by design, so deployment distributions may behave differently.
The forced-label intervention demonstrates control sensitivity but is partly tautological because labels map directly to policy classes.
The semantic-evidence follow-up is unavailable for one model due provider-side JSON validation, limiting cross-model symmetry.
